Retired probation officer Diana Salcedo had downsized to a home in Imperial’s Paseo del Sol neighborhood and was looking forward to a new chapter in her life caring for her mother and young grandchildren. Then Salcedo found out about a proposal to build what could be California’s largest data center across the street. articles.title: They Voted for Trump
articles.author: Gabriel Thompson
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On a sunny September afternoon, Juan Carlos stands behind the counter of his compact variety shop in California’s Central Valley, notes the lack of customers and pulls out a binder full of questions. During breaks, the slender 47-year-old is studying for his U.S. citizenship test. With business down 30% from a year ago, there’s plenty of time to study. “The other stores are also struggling,” he said. “Prices keep going up, so people are not spending.” Juan Carlos’ store, which sells a bit of everything — cowboy boots and piñatas, toiletries and backpacks — is in downtown Livingston, a small city in Merced County best known for its sprawling Foster Farms poultry plant and si

articles.title: Medicaid Cuts Pose Political Risk for Six-Term Congressman
articles.author: Elizabeth Aguilera
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Danielle Velling depends on monthly injections to keep her severe asthma at bay in California’s Central Valley, one of the most polluted regions in the U.S., where asthma rates exceed those in other parts of the state. She receives the medication thanks to Medicaid, the government-funded insurance program, known in California as Medi-Cal. But now she worries she could lose that insurance. Concern about cuts to health care prompted Velling, and dozens of others, to spend a record hot evening last month campaigning for upstart Democrat Randy Villegas. articles.title: Trump's One-Man Horror Show Continues
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Donald Trump is a one-man horror show. Call him “annihilation man” for threatening to exterminate nearly 93 million Iranians for the crime of defying his will (and that of Israel and Netanyahu). I don’t write about Trump a lot because he’s so scrutable. He is what he is, an utterly shameless con man, a bullying narcissist who’s always on the make. What he isn’t, what he’s never been, what he never will be, is a public servant. Sadly, he has a lot of company. articles.title: A New Israeli Government Won’t Stop the Settlements
articles.author: Diana Buttu
articles.content_excerpt: Next Tuesday, Israel will hold its first general election since the October 7 attacks and the destruction of Gaza. The election campaign has again illustrated the radicalization of Israeli politics, even beyond Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, and the breadth of political forces who staunchly resist the creation of a Palestinian state. In an interview, Palestinian Canadian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu, who lives in Haifa, explains why she will cast her ballot in this election while rejecting Israel’s claim to be a democracy. Speaking to Elias Feroz for Jacobin , she discusses what a change of government could — and could not — mean for Palestinians, the new death penalty law, and the planned Palestinian elections next month. articles.title: Brazil’s Far-Right Trajectory Is a Warning for Us All
articles.author: Rodrigo Nunes
articles.content_excerpt: Attempts to make generalizations from what happens in the United States and Europe to the rest of the planet do not, as a rule, meet with much surprise; these are, after all, generally assumed to be the most advanced edges of world history, where processes that will eventually spread to other regions first take hold. Most of the literature on the lethal danger surrounding democracies that has flourished in the last decade implicitly assumes these central countries as the normative standard from which others — and increasingly themselves — can be measured as deviations. Starting from a place like Brazil, on the other hand, does not enjoy the same air of self-evidence and seems to require some explaining. articles.title: Hyman Minsky Was a Powerful Critic of Capitalism
articles.author: Riccardo Bellofiore
articles.content_excerpt: Thirty years after Hyman Minsky’s death, his name is more familiar than his political economy. Whenever asset prices collapse, leverage suddenly matters, or a financial boom turns into panic, someone announces a new “Minsky moment.” The phrase has become shorthand for the point at which a speculative expansion can no longer sustain itself. Hedge finance turns into speculative finance, speculative finance into Ponzi finance, and a structure that appeared stable suddenly discovers that everybody cannot become liquid at the same time. This posthumous fame has narrowed our understanding of Minsky’s legacy . He was not primarily a prophet of crashes. articles.title: Israel’s Rogue State Behavior Is Somehow Only Worsening
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: I t is not a novel point that Israel acts like a rogue state , or that its behavior toward the United States often more closely resembles the behavior of an adversary than that of an ally. But it’s still worth periodically noting just how extreme its misbehavior on the world stage is, given that it is underwritten by the US taxpayers, even as majorities of Americans don’t want it to be. articles.title: There’s No End in Sight to Yemen’s Destructive War
articles.author: Helen Lackner
articles.content_excerpt: Yet again, the world is failing to give Yemen the attention it deserves. Well over a month into the renewal of the war between Ansar Allah, known as the Huthis, and the internationally recognized government (IRG), there have already been thousands of military and civilian casualties on both sides. Fierce fighting is going on in different parts of the country, and more than 250,000 people have been displaced, most of whom are moving from one active front line to areas that might be swept up in the conflict within hours. The humanitarian situation is disastrous, with famine threatening in some parts of the country. articles.title: Milwaukee’s Proud History of Baseball — and Socialism
articles.author: Peter Dreier
articles.content_excerpt: Organizers like to say that all politics boils down to a battle between organized money and organized people. Candidates with the largest war chests tend to win, but contenders who refuse to take donations from corporate interests can prevail if their supporters are well-organized, inspired, and strategic. Likewise, big employers can spend huge sums on union busting, but employees can win union organizing drives if they know how to mobilize workers to stick together and not be intimidated. The same is true in baseball. Teams in big markets with large payrolls have a decided advantage when it comes to recruiting talented players who command huge salaries, but feisty, scrappy teams with fewer stars can sometimes win championships. articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Recently, a friend asked whether I had seen the documentary Natchez . Knowing of my involvement in Coming to the Table , he sent a link, encouraged me to watch, and asked whether I would write about it afterward. Coming to the Table brings together descendants of enslaved people and enslavers, along with others committed to racial justice, to uncover history, build relationships, pursue healing, and take action. Through that work, I have come to know Tom DeWolf, a founding member and longtime leader. articles.title: Vancouver Is in the Middle of a Socialist Surge
articles.author: James Adair
articles.content_excerpt: Vancouver’s contrasts are visible on its streets. Luxury cars cruise past some of North America’s worst homeless encampments. Last Saturday, October 17, the city produced a political contrast to match: after four years of a center-right city hall, its municipal council has transformed into one of the most left-wing in North America. The breakthrough comes alongside strong socialist showings in municipal elections around the world, from Zohran Mamdani’s win in New York to Die Linke’s recent state election victory in Berlin. The Coalition of Progressive Electors (COPE), a democratic socialist party, elected all twelve candidates it ran: four to council, four to school board, and four to park board. articles.title: It’s the Rent, Actually
articles.content_excerpt: Deanna Muz, a retired nurse living in Saginaw, Mich., has typically voted Republican. But with ​ “ the way our economy is and all the BS going on,” she says, ​ “ I’m in that ​ ‘ I’m not sure’ phase.” Chief among Muz’s economic concerns is her housing — specifically, the sale of her manufactured home community to the private equity firm Brookfield Asset Management, and the possibility that subsequent rent and fee increases will force her to leave. In other words, she’s the kind of voter Democrats might hope to woo with an appeal to affordability, the political watchword of the moment. But for millions of struggling renters, that appeal may still sound fuzzy, at best. articles.title: A Sweeping Reelection Victory for Shawn Fain and His Slate at UAW
articles.content_excerpt: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain is poised to win a second four-year term, with an overwhelming lead in member balloting for the union’s top officers. The election was a referendum on the new fighting direction Fain has taken the union by leading 2023 ’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, other bold contract fights and new organizing campaigns. It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021 . Fain took more than two-thirds of the vote, against five opponents. His nearest competitor, incumbent vice president Rich Boyer, had around 13 %. Fain is running as part of the United UAW slate. articles.title: “They’re Trying to Starve Us”: BP Opposes Unemployment Benefits for Locked-Out Workers
articles.content_excerpt: WHITING, IND.— Six and a half months after being locked out of his job as a British Petroleum (BP) operator, Jon is still showing up to picket shifts. I met him on the side of a road, the refinery spewing smoke behind him. For a while, unemployment benefits of around $ 335 a week helped ease the financial burden, he tells me, but those went away at the end of September when he hit the six-month mark. And now, BP is appealing the locked-out workers’ unemployment with the state of Indiana. It’s a move that could result in workers like Jon having to pay back the assistance they’ve already received. articles.title: From the Green Line to the Yellow Line: A Story of Colonization in Palestine
articles.content_excerpt: In October 2025 , a ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Palestinian factions was supposed to bring calm to a Gaza devastated by genocide. Instead, Israel has continued to violate the ceasefire, murdering more than a thousand Palestinians since the agreement began and usurping more land via the ​ “ yellow line” — an arbitrary line splitting the Gaza Strip into eastern and western halves. A year since the ceasefire, Israel has continued to push the yellow line inwards and now controls nearly 70 percent of the Gaza Strip and continues to kill Palestinians on a daily basis simply for being near the arbitrary line.
